title: Where the Energy Goes — Feeding an Ecosystem

info.text: How energy enters an ecosystem through autotrophs, who eats whom across trophic levels, why each transfer loses most of the energy — and why that taper concentrates toxins at the top.

links.label: OpenStax Biology 2e §46.2 Energy Flow through Ecosystems

clusters.name: The Base: Making Food
clusters.fact: Every ecosystem's energy enters through organisms that build their own food — from sunlight almost everywhere, or from chemistry in the dark — and only part of what they capture stays available.

termInfo.autotroph: An organism that makes its own organic food from inorganic sources — literally ‘self-feeder’. Every ecosystem's energy budget starts with them.
termInfo.photoautotroph: An autotroph powered by sunlight: plants, algae, and cyanobacteria. Phytoplankton alone do about 40% of Earth's photosynthesis.
termInfo.chemoautotroph: An autotroph powered by chemical bonds instead of light — bacteria at deep-sea hydrothermal vents, 2.5 km down, run whole communities without a photon.
termInfo.gross primary productivity: All the energy autotrophs capture per unit time — the ecosystem's gross income.
termInfo.net primary productivity: What remains of gross productivity after the autotrophs' own respiration — the actual budget available to every consumer above them.

info.text: Autotrophs make organic compounds from inorganic sources: photoautotrophs — plants, algae, cyanobacteria — use sunlight (about 40% of Earth's photosynthesis is done by phytoplankton); chemoautotrophs run on chemical bonds at hydrothermal vents, 2.5 km down where no light reaches. Gross primary productivity is everything they capture; net primary productivity is what remains after their own respiration — the budget every consumer lives on.

clusters.name: Everyone Else: Eating to Live
clusters.fact: Heterotrophs get their energy by eating others — plants, animals, both, or what's already dead — and each role is a different way of living off the producers' budget.

termInfo.heterotroph: An organism that must eat other organisms for energy — literally ‘other-feeder’. Every other role here is a heterotroph's specialty.
termInfo.herbivore: Eats plants or algae — the primary consumer, the first bite of the producers' work.
termInfo.carnivore: Eats other animals — the secondary and higher consumers of a chain.
termInfo.omnivore: Eats both plants and animals; the opossum shrimp eats phytoplankton and copepods alike — which is exactly why food webs, not chains, tell the truth.
termInfo.decomposer: Feeds on decaying matter, breaking down dead organisms and wastes (openly, alongside fellow detritivores). The base of the detrital food web.

info.text: Heterotrophs cannot make their own food. Herbivores eat plants (the primary consumers), carnivores eat other animals, omnivores — like the opossum shrimp — eat both. Decomposers (with their fellow detritivores) feed on decaying matter, breaking down dead organisms and wastes; without them every ecosystem would drown in its own detritus.

clusters.name: Mapping Who Eats Whom
clusters.fact: A single line of who-eats-whom is a chain; the tangled reality is a web; each rung of either is a trophic level — and real omnivory is why the web wins.

termInfo.food chain: One linear who-eats-whom sequence: phytoplankton → copepod → fish → squid → shark.
termInfo.food web: The holistic network of every chain in an ecosystem — what reality looks like once omnivores feed across levels.
termInfo.trophic level: One rung of the feeding structure — primary producers, primary consumers, and so on — the unit the pyramids count.
termInfo.grazing food web: The web built on living tissue, rooted in plants or other photosynthesizers.
termInfo.detrital food web: The web built on decaying matter, based on decomposers and detritivores; most grazing webs have one as a twin.
termInfo.apex consumer: The carnivore at the top of the chain that nothing else eats.

info.text: A food chain is one linear sequence — phytoplankton to copepod to fish to squid to shark. A food web is the holistic map of all chains, because organisms like omnivores feed at several levels. Each position is a trophic level. Grazing food webs start from living plants or photosynthesizers; detrital food webs start from decaying matter — most ecosystems have both, running side by side. The top rung is the apex consumer, the carnivore nothing else eats.

clusters.name: Why Energy Runs Out
clusters.fact: Each trophic level keeps only a fraction of the last one's energy — so pyramids of energy can never flip, and toxins that don't leave the body climb the same staircase in ever-higher doses.

termInfo.ecological pyramid: A chart of amounts across trophic levels — of numbers, of biomass, or of energy; only the energy version is always upright.
termInfo.trophic level transfer efficiency: The share of one level's energy that the next level actually receives — about 14.8% from producers to primary consumers at Silver Springs; roughly 10% is the rule of thumb.
termInfo.biomass: The total mass of living or recently living tissue per unit area — the currency the biomass pyramid weighs.
termInfo.biomagnification: Persistent toxins concentrate with each step up the chain: DDT rose from water to apex birds and thinned their eggshells.

info.text: An ecological pyramid shows the amounts at each trophic level — of numbers, of biomass (the mass of living and recently living tissue), or of energy. Only the energy pyramid is always upright, because transfers lose most of what they receive: trophic level transfer efficiency at Silver Springs, Florida ran about 14.8% from producers to primary consumers, and roughly 10% is the rule of thumb. By the tertiary consumers, 20,810 kcal/m²/yr had dwindled to 21. Biomagnification is the shadow side: persistent toxins like DDT don't dissolve away, so each level concentrates what the level below ate — apex predators inherit the largest dose.

bridges.term: every web starts at the producers
bridges.fact: The bottom rung of every food chain and grazing food web is photosynthetic organisms — the primary producers — which is why a web can't be drawn until someone names what makes the food: phytoplankton, grass, or the chemosynthetic bacteria of a vent community.

info.text: OpenStax 46.1: the base of many food chains consists of photosynthetic organisms; grazing webs have plants or other photosynthesizers at their base.

bridges.term: two webs run side by side
bridges.fact: Ecosystems generally show two overlapping webs: the grazing food web, built from living tissue and starting at producers, and the detrital food web, built from decaying matter and based on decomposers and detritivores — most grazing webs have a detrital twin, and the two share many consumers.

info.text: OpenStax 46.1: most grazing food webs have an associated detrital food web whose base is decomposers and detritivores.

bridges.term: counted by level, lost per transfer
bridges.fact: Trophic levels are where the pyramid counts — and each transfer between them is where the count falls: with transfer efficiency near 10%, energy shrinks about tenfold per rung, which is why food chains rarely pass four to six transfers and why nothing outranks the apex consumer for long.

info.text: OpenStax 46.2: Silver Springs producers held 20,810 kcal/m²/yr; tertiary consumers held 21 — a trophic level transfer efficiency of about 14.8% for that first step.

lenses.prompt: Two board terms name the two kinds of autotroph by energy source. Which two?
lenses.explanation: The two source-specialists; autotroph itself is the umbrella over them, so the bounded wording 'kinds by energy source' excludes it.

reasons.chemoautotroph: Runs on chemical bonds — vent communities.
reasons.photoautotroph: Runs on sunlight — plants, algae, cyanobacteria.

lenses.prompt: Three board terms name eating roles that differ only by what living thing they eat — plants, animals, or both. Which three?
lenses.explanation: Bounded by living food: decomposer eats what's already dead and heterotroph is the umbrella, so only the three diet roles answer.

reasons.omnivore: Eats both — which is why webs beat chains.

lenses.prompt: Two board terms name an ecosystem's twin maps — one built on living tissue, one on decaying matter. Which two?
lenses.explanation: The twin webs are the only terms built on where the web's matter comes from; chain and web are general structures, not matter-based halves.

reasons.detrital food web: Rooted in decomposers feeding on decaying matter.
reasons.grazing food web: Rooted in living plants and photosynthesizers.

lenses.prompt: Which board term names the measure of how much energy survives one step up the chain?
lenses.explanation: Net primary productivity measures the base, not a step; biomass is a stock, not a ratio; only TLTE is the per-transfer measure.

reasons.trophic level transfer efficiency: About 10% rule of thumb; 14.8% at Silver Springs' first step.

lenses.prompt: Which board term names the process by which a persistent toxin grows more concentrated at each step up the chain?
lenses.explanation: The taper's shadow side: biomagnification is the only term about concentration rather than energy quantity.

reasons.biomagnification: DDT concentrated upward until it thinned apex birds' eggshells.

learningIntroduction.title: Where the energy goes
learningIntroduction.summary: How energy enters ecosystems through autotrophs, passes along eating roles and web structures, and why ~10% transfer efficiency shapes pyramids, chains, and toxins alike.

content.text:
Trace any meal back far enough and you arrive at sunlight — or, in a few strange places, at chemistry. Energy flow through an ecosystem is the story of that trace: where energy enters, who passes it along, and why so little of it survives the trip.

The story starts with the autotrophs — literally "self-feeders" — organisms that build organic food from inorganic raw materials. Almost all of them are **photoautotrophs**: plants, algae, and cyanobacteria running on sunlight; drifting phytoplankton alone account for roughly 40 percent of Earth's photosynthesis. In the dark a mile and a half under the ocean, **chemoautotrophs** do the same job with chemical bonds instead of light, anchoring whole communities at hydrothermal vents. Ecologists measure what the base makes: **gross primary productivity** is everything captured; **net primary productivity** is what remains after the producers run their own metabolism — the only part of the budget anyone else can spend.

Everyone above the base is a **heterotroph** — an "other-feeder" — and each plays a role defined by what it eats. **Herbivores** eat plants (they are a chain's primary consumers); **carnivores** eat animals; **omnivores** eat both; and **decomposers** — with their fellow detritivores — feed on what's already dead, breaking down remains and wastes that would otherwise bury the world.

These roles connect into structures. A **food chain** is one straight line of who-eats-whom: phytoplankton → copepod → fish → squid → shark. Reality is rarely straight, because omnivores like the opossum shrimp feed on both phytoplankton and copepods, so ecologists draw the **food web** — every chain at once. Each position in either picture is a **trophic level**, and ecosystems generally run two webs side by side: the **grazing food web**, built on living tissue and rooted in photosynthesizers, and the **detrital food web**, built on decaying matter and based on decomposers. At the very top sits the **apex consumer**, the predator nothing else eats.

Here is the cruel arithmetic: every transfer up the staircase loses most of the energy it carries. Some of what an animal eats is never digested; most of what is digested becomes heat through respiration, because organisms are warm, busy machines. The **trophic level transfer efficiency** — about 15 percent at Howard Odum's famous Silver Springs study, and near 10 percent as a rule of thumb — means only a tenth of each rung's energy reaches the next. At Silver Springs the producers held 20,810 kilocalories per square meter per year; the tertiary consumers held 21. That arithmetic is why **ecological pyramids** of energy are always upright, why food chains rarely run more than four to six transfers, why apex predators are rare — and why a grassland can carry millions of rabbits but only a handful of hawks.

The taper has a darker echo. A persistent toxin like DDT doesn't leave the body, so each level's consumers collect everything the level below ever ate: the poison **biomagnifies**, and the apex predator — already the rarest animal on the staircase — inherits the largest dose of all.
